articles.title: Bob Mackie, costume designer to stars daring to be noticed, dies aged 87
articles.summary: Famous for his flamboyant outfits, he helped celebrities including Cher, Tina Turner and Elton John cause a stir. Bob Mackie, the costume designer behind some of the most sexy and glamorous outfits worn by celebrities in the past 50 years, has died at the age of 87.
body: “He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a fashion and costume designer, which is all he ever wanted to do,” read a statement posted on his Instagram account. “His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world.”

Mackie’s work can be seen in the wardrobes of stars ranging from Marilyn Monroe to Carol Burnett, Liza Minnelli, Elton John, Dolly Parton, Tina Turner and – perhaps most memorably – Cher. He designed the ‘naked’ dress the singer wore to attend the Met Gala in 1975, the midriff-baring outfit with an oversized Mohawk headdress she wore to the Oscars in 1986 and the transparent body stocking she wore for the If I Could Turn Back Time video in 1989.
The Met Gala outfit has since become a reference for a younger generation. Kim Kardashian wore a dress modelled on it for the same event in 2015.
points: Famous for his flamboyant outfits, he helped celebrities including Cher, Tina Turner and Elton John cause a stir.
Bob Mackie, the costume designer behind some of the most sexy and glamorous outfits worn by celebrities in the past 50 years, has died at the age of 87.

articles.title: ‘It’s about controlling your entire body’: how to start doing handstands
articles.summary: Handstands display a mastery of one’s physical form that I have never quite felt – and they look cool. Experts share their advice for building up strength and practicing.
body: M y aspirations in life are modest: I want to write, spend time with my loved ones, and someday find a lipstick that flatters my skintone. But perhaps my greatest ambition is this: I want to be able to do a handstand.

Why? It turns the world upside down. It seems fun. It displays a mastery of one’s physical form that I have never quite felt. And it looks cool! Maybe it has to do with that one time in third grade when all my friends could do a handstand and I couldn’t, but that’s for me and my therapist to sort out later.

A handstand is an inversion, a type of position where one’s heart is above the head. Besides looking cool, there is a lot to gain from inversions. When the head is below the heart, oxygen-rich blood flow to the brain increases, according to the UC Irvine Integrative Health Institute. This helps “regulate neurotransmitters and nourish brain cells”. Other benefits include stress reduction and increased physical strength and mobility, says Antoinette Webb, a registered yoga teacher.
“A handstand is a full-body inversion in which you support your weight through your hands while balancing upside down,” says Frank Medrano, a calisthenics athlete and coach.

articles.title: Hard truths about solo homeownership – and the tools that made these women DIY pros
articles.summary: Women who have tackled home repairs and renovations share hard-earned tips and tools that helped them patch drywall, refinish floors and build decks. 11 products our writers rely on to organize and declutter. Sign up for the Filter US newsletter, your weekly guide to buying fewer, better things.
body: I entered homeownership the same way I started driving on the highway: learning on the fly and in a blind panic. I bought my house in my late 20s, with minimal home-maintenance knowledge, a flathead screwdriver, a rubber mallet that had lived through the Carter administration – and the realization that throughout my life, I had been spared from doing the dirty work at the cost of learning how it was done.

Before owning a home, I might have taken him at his word. There was a time when hanging drywall and cutting tile would have seemed well beyond the bounds of my own competence. But now, when people walk into my house, one of their first questions is often: “Who taught you how to do all this?” The answer is … a lot of people. I’ve just never met any of them. I cobbled my education together from online tutorials, Reddit threads and a lot of trial and error.

articles.title: Milamore and Juju Vera Brought a Moment of Calm–and Lots of Diamonds–to NYFW
articles.summary: Two jewelry designers are among this year’s 10 CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund Finalists, and both hosted New York Fashion Week presentations: Milamore, by designer George Inaki, at a traditional Japanese tea house, and Juju Ferentinos’s label Juju Vera at her brand-new studio.
body: On Friday, Inaki gathered the fashion set for ceremonial matcha at Sorate. Inaki, who is of Spanish-Filipino and Japanese heritage, wanted to show visitors a bit of his culture, while also showing off his new collection. Milamore is based around Kintsugi, the Japanese practice of repairing broken pottery by filling the cracks with gold lacquer—with many of the pieces sculpted to look like the gilded seams that hold the pottery together.

“It all started with the idea of wanting to mend myself. When I moved from Japan I didn’t have friends, I didn’t have a job, I came to this big city of dreams to become someone, but I really struggled,” Inaki said.

Tea masters don’t typically wear jewelry, but Sorate’s made an exception. She wore the brand’s signature Kintsugi necklace, a gold squiggle that sits at the collarbone, as well as one of Inaki’s newer creations—kimonos upcycled into shirts with pearl and diamond buttons. Inaki also showed off a heart pendant and his silver puzzle chain necklace, its interlocking hooks made to be completely broken apart and then put back together at the wearer’s whim.

articles.title: This Season’s Unlikely LFW It Piece? The British Museum’s Bayeux Tapestry Merch
articles.summary: No, I haven’t yet secured a ticket to the British Museum’s wildly popular Bayeux Tapestry exhibition—but have I have added some of its merch to my cart? Yes!
body: Have you ever tried buying a Glastonbury ticket? Or tried to get a Centre Court seat on finals day at Wimbledon? Were you one of the millions frantically refreshing your browser to secure a spot at the Eras Tour? Well, consider those practice runs. The final boss of hard-to-get tickets landed this July, when slots for the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum went on sale.

It isn’t hard to understand why the show is so feverishly popular: the exceptionally fragile 70-meter stretch of 11th-century embroidery, depicting the historical events surrounding 1066 and the Battle of Hastings—arguably the central moment in Britain’s national mythology—was most likely stitched by skilled Anglo-Saxon needlewomen based in Canterbury, yet has spent the best part of a millennium housed in Normandy. While the museum there undergoes a renovation, the tapestry has been shipped back to England with the utmost care, where it has already received visitors including King Charles and the Macrons. It is, to put it mildly, a very big deal.

articles.title: I Spent Four Days Touring Scotland’s Whisky Island—and It Was Better Than I Expected
articles.summary: One writer's experience taking a small-group tour of Islay with her dad, visiting historic distilleries, sampling smoky drams, and discovering why the island is worth the journey.
body: My dad’s 60th birthday was coming up, and as an avid whisky drinker with a particularly sharp nose, his dream trip has always been to explore the coastline of Islay, a Scottish island famed worldwide for its smoky, peated single malt whiskies. I often travel solo and am fond of organized tours, so when I came across Rabbie’s four-day Islay and whisky tour —with pickup from Edinburgh, a selection of historic stops, a maximum group size of 16 people, and plenty of opportunities for drams—it sounded ideal for us both.

Islay is the southernmost island of the Inner Hebrides, with a landscape of rugged beaches and peat bogs, and traveling through it usually involves many small logistics. I was thrilled to see that this tour handles all of the planning for you—including transportation, accommodations, attractions, and providing a local guide for the four-day trip. It starts at just $609 per adult without accommodations or distillery tours, or around $1,464 all-in, which seemed like a great deal. I was convinced, so I booked it!

articles.title: The Case for Taking Kids on Big Trips—Even Those That Sound Like a Terrible Idea
articles.summary: One writer counts safaris, Mardi Gras, and an India excursion among her mother-toddler trips. Here's why she has rarely, if ever, regretted it.
body: I have a long track record of making ill-advised—occasionally unhinged—family-travel decisions. My son Julian’s first interstate trip was to Wisconsin to go ice fishing at five weeks old. At 20 months, I took him—just the two of us—on a 23-day trip through Oman, Tanzania, and the United Arab Emirates to road trip across the Wahiba Sands and Hajar Mountains before flying off on safari. Friends thought I’d lost it. My husband wished me luck and stayed home.

A year later, Julian and I left for 88 days and 14 countries across six continents. Our stint in India, which set off alarm bells with family, was one of my favorite stops: In the glorious sensory overload of Varanasi and Delhi, Julian’s loudness barely registered; I could finally exhale.

I waited a long time to have a child because I wasn’t sure I wanted one—or was particularly cut out to be somebody’s mom. Parenthood has changed how I assess risk, but fear has never gotten much of a vote in my life, and I don’t want it calling the shots in his either. Sometimes the whole thing blows up in your face. But I’ve learned not to confuse a hard trip with a bad one.

articles.title: At Nihi Rote and Hospitality Academy, Exploring Eastern Indonesia by Boat and Board
articles.summary: A far cry from Bali, the remote Indonesian island has long been a go-to amongst surfers. Now, Nihi Rote and Hospitality Academy is ushering in a new crowd of quiet-seekers.
body: There are not many places left in the world like the tip of Rote. It’s a fragment of coastline on an island off West Timor, which itself is a far-flung extremity of the eastern Indonesian archipelago, closer to Darwin than Jakarta. Aussie surfers started coming here 40-odd years ago, arriving for Rote’s long, clean waves, magicked up by a rare blend of wind, swell, and bathymetry.

There are other elements that give Rote its dream-come-true energy: tropical weather, white sand beaches, dense fringes of coconut palms, lingering sunsets, a steady trade wind in the dry season that keeps the mosquitoes down. Rote is, alluringly, always on island time. Crucially, it’s not easy to reach—good for surfers who don’t much like sharing a wave. The long journey to get here is why Rote has stayed Rote, one of the most wonderfully inconvenient places out there.

Now, Nihi Rote and Hospitality Academy is ushering in a new crowd of quiet-seekers.

articles.title: D.C.’s Most Exciting New Restaurant Started as a Pop-Up
articles.summary: This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews. Now Open is a yearlong series celebrating some of 2026’s most exciting new restaurants.
body: When chefs Justin Ahn and Alex McCoy opened Alfie’s as a pop-up restaurant in 2016, they didn’t expect the road to a brick-and-mortar location to last nearly a decade. The temporary D.C. location where the duo served northern Thai cuisine to the city’s tight-knit service industry and other regulars was open for just a few months. After that, Ahn and McCoy began operating it as a roving concept all around the world, but now they’re finally returning to D.C. with a permanent venue in Georgetown.

Now the team is settled into a new 25-seat venue tucked in an alley off of Georgetown’s M Street serving Thai dishes made with Mid-Atlantic ingredients and natural wine produced just over the river in Virginia. Still, elements of the pop-up — like its run-and-gun service and chalkboard menu that shifts based on what local purveyors have in season — remain. We caught up with McCoy to learn more about how the team has shifted this scrappy pop-up model into a brick-and-mortar concept while keeping that dynamic energy intact.
Liz Provencher: Why did you decide to launch Alfie’s in a pop-up format?
